curriculum_source: CFA Program 2027 Level III Volume 1, Learning Module 3

drills.los_text: describe elements of effective investment governance and investment governance considerations in asset allocation

questions.stem: The distinction between governance and management of an investment program is best described as:

options.A: governance clarifying the mission and reviewing progress, management executing the plan.
options.B: identical activities assigned to different people.
options.C: governance executing the plan, management clarifying the mission.

rationales.A: Governance is the function of clarifying the mission, establishing the objectives of the investment program and the plan to reach them, and reviewing progress toward those objectives. Management efforts are geared to outcomes — the execution of that plan within the decision rights governance has allocated.
rationales.B: Governance and management are two separate but related functions, not one set of activities carried out by two groups. Governance sets the mission, allocates decision rights and monitors progress; management executes within those bounds, so the activities themselves differ.
rationales.C: This reverses the two functions. Clarifying the mission and creating the plan is governance, not management, and executing the plan is management, not governance.

questions.stem: A task performed under an effective investment governance model is most likely:

options.A: managing individual security selection at the committee level.
options.B: undertaking a periodic governance audit.
options.C: selecting benchmarks at the investment staff level exclusively.

rationales.A: Selection of individual securities is properly delegated to outside managers or to investment staff. A committee that retains security selection has taken on an implementation task rather than a governance task, which is what the allocation of decision rights is meant to prevent.
rationales.B: The six common elements of an effective investment governance model are: articulating the long- and short-term objectives of the investment program; allocating decision rights and responsibilities among the functional units according to their skills and capacity; specifying a process for developing and approving the investment policy statement; specifying a process for developing and approving the strategic asset allocation; establishing a reporting framework to monitor the program's progress toward its objectives; and periodically undertaking a governance audit.
rationales.C: Benchmark selection is not retained exclusively by investment staff. It is a shared responsibility spanning the investment committee, staff and third-party consultants, with the committee approving benchmarks that staff and consultants propose.

questions.stem: Approval of the asset allocation policy most likely resides with the:

options.A: investment staff, with committee ratification.
options.B: external consultants, with committee sign-off.
options.C: investment committee, with input from staff and consultants.

rationales.A: Investment staff drafts the asset allocation policy, with input from consultants, but approval is not a staff function. The committee approves the policy itself rather than ratifying a decision staff has already taken.
rationales.B: Consultants supply input to the drafting of the policy. They hold no approval authority, and an external adviser cannot approve the fund's own policy.
rationales.C: Approval of the asset allocation policy resides with the investment committee, acting on input from investment staff and from external consultants. Staff drafts the policy with consultant input; the committee, which holds that decision right, approves it.

questions.curriculum_ref: Exhibit 2: Allocation of Rights and Responsibilities

questions.stem: An IPS should be structured with a stable foundation document that is revised slowly over time and a more easily modified appendix. Content typically placed in the appendix would most likely include:

options.A: the philosophy and long-term investment beliefs.
options.B: the asset allocation policy and manager guidelines.
options.C: the mission statement of the fund.

rationales.A: Investment philosophy and long-term investment beliefs are stable. They belong in the foundation document, which is revised slowly over time.
rationales.B: The IPS itself is a foundation document, revised slowly over time. Information relating to the more variable aspects of the program — the asset allocation policy and the guidelines for individual investment managers — is placed in an appendix that can be modified more easily as managers, markets and capital market expectations change.
rationales.C: The mission statement is the most stable element of the whole document and sits in the foundation document, not the appendix.

questions.stem: The three questions answered by an effective reporting framework most likely concern:

options.A: current position, progress against objectives, and value added by management.
options.B: responsibility, timeline, and budget.
options.C: returns, risk, and fees.

rationales.A: A reporting framework should answer three questions clearly and concisely: Where are we now? Where are we relative to the goals and objectives of the investment program? And what value has been added or subtracted by management decisions? Reporting built around these three supports effective monitoring of the program's progress.
rationales.B: Responsibility, timeline and budget are questions about governance structure and the subject matter of a governance audit. They are not the questions the reporting framework is designed to answer.
rationales.C: Returns, risk and fees are inputs that appear in performance reporting, but they are components of performance evaluation rather than the three framing questions a reporting framework answers.

questions.stem: The purpose of a governance audit is most likely to:

options.A: ensure policies, procedures, and governance structures are effective.
options.B: verify the accuracy of the financial statements.
options.C: evaluate manager performance against the benchmarks.

rationales.A: A governance audit ensures that the established policies, procedures and governance structures of the investment program are effective. To be credible it should be performed by an independent third party, and it is undertaken periodically as one of the elements of an effective governance model.
rationales.B: Verifying the accuracy of the financial statements is the purpose of a financial audit. A governance audit examines structures, policies and procedures, not the statements.
rationales.C: Evaluating manager performance against the benchmarks is part of performance evaluation and reporting, a separate activity from the governance audit.

questions.stem: Decision-reversal risk most likely refers to the risk of:

options.A: a committee overturning a staff-level decision.
options.B: reversing a course of action at the point of maximum loss.
options.C: an auditor recommending reversal of a prior allocation.

rationales.A: A committee overturning a staff-level decision is a question of decision rights and escalation within the governance structure. It is not decision-reversal risk as defined.
rationales.B: Decision-reversal risk is the risk of reversing a chosen course of action at exactly the wrong time — the point of maximum loss. It typically arises when a decision maker abandons a long-horizon policy after short-term losses. Good governance seeks to avoid it by allocating decision rights to those with the skill, capacity and time to exercise them, and by documenting the policy in advance so that it is not reconsidered under stress.
rationales.C: An auditor recommending that a prior asset allocation be reversed is a governance-audit finding. It is not the risk of abandoning a course of action at the point of maximum loss.

questions.stem: Governance at a sovereign wealth fund is most likely questionable when:

options.A: the CIO builds a staff organization with a head for each major asset class.
options.B: staff drafts the asset allocation policy and the committee approves it.
options.C: the investment committee is deeply involved in individual manager selection.

rationales.A: A chief investment officer who builds a staff organization with heads for each major asset class is following sound practice. It places implementation skill and capacity where the implementation decisions are made.
rationales.B: The division in which investment staff drafts the asset allocation policy with consultant input and the investment committee approves it is sound practice. It matches the allocation of decision rights an effective governance model calls for.
rationales.C: An investment committee deeply involved in the selection and evaluation of individual managers is questionable practice. Manager selection and evaluation reside more effectively with investment staff, who have the skill, capacity and time to carry them out; the committee's role is strategy and oversight, not implementation.

drills.los_text: formulate an economic balance sheet for a client and interpret its implications for asset allocation

questions.stem: An economic balance sheet differs from a conventional accounting balance sheet most likely by:

options.A: including only financial assets and liabilities.
options.B: also including extended portfolio assets and liabilities.
options.C: excluding liabilities entirely.

rationales.A: The economic balance sheet includes more than financial assets and liabilities, not fewer. Restricting it to financial items would leave the conventional accounting balance sheet.
rationales.B: An economic balance sheet includes the conventional assets and liabilities plus extended portfolio assets and liabilities that do not appear on a conventional accounting balance sheet but are relevant to the asset allocation decision — for an individual, human capital and the present value of pension income; for an institution, items such as the present value of future intellectual property royalties or of expected future donations.
rationales.C: The economic balance sheet includes liabilities: both the financial liabilities of the conventional balance sheet and extended liabilities such as the present value of future consumption for an individual or of future pension payments for an institution.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Economic Balance Sheet and Asset Allocation

questions.stem: For an individual investor, extended portfolio assets most likely include:

options.A: human capital, pension income, and expected inheritances.
options.B: publicly traded stocks and mutual fund positions.
options.C: checking account balances and money market funds.

rationales.A: Extended portfolio assets for an individual investor are human capital, the present value of future earnings from employment; the present value of expected pension income; and the present value of expected inheritances. None appears on a conventional balance sheet, yet each is relevant to the asset allocation decision.
rationales.B: Publicly traded stock holdings and mutual fund positions are conventional financial assets, already shown on the conventional balance sheet. They are not extended portfolio assets.
rationales.C: Checking account balances and money market funds are conventional financial assets, recorded on the conventional balance sheet rather than added as extended assets.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Economic Balance Sheet and Asset Allocation

questions.stem: For an individual investor, the present value of future consumption is most likely classified as:

options.A: A financial asset.
options.B: An extended portfolio asset.
options.C: An extended portfolio liability.

rationales.A: Future consumption is a claim against the individual's total wealth, not a resource available to meet claims. Treating it as a financial asset would also double-count, because the resources that fund consumption, financial capital and human capital, already sit on the asset side of the extended economic balance sheet.
rationales.B: The present value of future consumption does belong on the extended economic balance sheet, but on the liability side. It is an obligation that must be funded out of financial capital and human capital rather than a resource that adds to economic net worth, so calling it an extended portfolio asset places it on the wrong side of the balance sheet.
rationales.C: On an individual's extended economic balance sheet, the present value of future consumption is an extended portfolio liability, alongside items such as the present value of future real estate liabilities. Extended liabilities are quasi-liabilities that a conventional balance sheet omits but that must still be funded from total economic wealth, which includes human capital and other extended assets. Economic net worth is economic assets minus economic liabilities, so recognizing future consumption reduces the net worth available for other objectives.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Economic Balance Sheet and Asset Allocation

questions.stem: On average, human capital is most likely characterized as:

options.A: 30% equity-like and 70% bond-like.
options.B: 70% equity-like and 30% bond-like.
options.C: 50% equity-like and 50% bond-like.

rationales.A: Research by Blanchett and Straehl indicates that on average human capital is roughly 30% equity-like and 70% bond-like. Labor income for most workers is comparatively stable and only loosely linked to equity market outcomes, so the bond-like component dominates, with significant variation across industries and occupations.
rationales.B: This reverses the estimated proportions. A 70% equity-like average would imply that most workers' labor income co-moves with equity markets nearly as strongly as equities themselves. That is true of some industries, but the cross-industry average is closer to 30% equity-like, because the bulk of labor income behaves like a bond-like stream of payments.
rationales.C: An even split overstates the equity-like component. The average estimate is roughly 30% equity-like and 70% bond-like, reflecting the relative stability of most labor income; industry-level estimates vary widely around that average, but the average itself is not balanced.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Economic Balance Sheet and Asset Allocation

questions.stem: Life-cycle balanced (target date) funds most likely increase the allocation to bonds over an investor's life because:

options.A: human capital, which is bond-like, declines with age.
options.B: regulation requires it as investors approach retirement.
options.C: bonds have outperformed equities over long horizons.

rationales.A: If risk tolerance is approximately constant through life, the asset allocation of total economic wealth, human capital plus financial capital, should also be approximately constant. Human capital is predominantly bond-like and declines as the investor ages and converts it into financial capital, so the financial portfolio must shift toward bonds to hold the total mix stable. That shift is the glide path a life-cycle balanced or target date fund implements.
rationales.B: The glide path is an economic argument, not a regulatory requirement. No rule obliges a target date fund to raise its bond weight as the investor ages; the fund does so because the bond-like share of total economic wealth shrinks as human capital is consumed over the working life.
rationales.C: Bonds have not consistently outperformed equities over long horizons, and relative performance is not the rationale in any case. The glide path rests on keeping the asset mix of total wealth, human plus financial capital, approximately constant while bond-like human capital declines, which would hold even if equities were expected to outperform throughout.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Economic Balance Sheet and Asset Allocation

questions.stem: A university endowment holds Class B real estate in the same regional market in which the university itself owns far larger real estate assets. On an extended economic balance sheet, the endowment's real estate holding is most likely concerning because:

options.A: it is stressed by the same conditions as the university's own real estate.
options.B: it is too illiquid to hold within the endowment's policy allocation.
options.C: it is too small a share of total assets to diversify meaningfully.

rationales.A: The value and income of the endowment's Class B real estate are likely to be stressed by the same local economic conditions that stress the university's much larger real estate holdings. Viewed on the extended economic balance sheet, which combines the sponsor's economic assets with the endowment portfolio, the two positions are highly correlated, so the endowment's real estate is far less diversifying than it appears when the endowment is analyzed in isolation, and the allocation may need re-examination.
rationales.B: Illiquidity is a general feature of direct real estate and is one that an endowment with a long horizon and a modest, predictable spending rate can usually tolerate; it is not a reason to exclude real estate from a policy allocation. The concern here is not liquidity but the correlation between the endowment's real estate and the sponsoring university's own, much larger, real estate exposure.
rationales.C: The concern is not the size of the position but its correlation. Because the endowment's real estate is stressed by the same local conditions as the university's much larger holdings, even a modest allocation adds concentrated exposure to a risk that already dominates the extended balance sheet, rather than adding diversification. Enlarging the allocation would worsen the problem instead of solving it.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Economic Balance Sheet of Auldberg University Endowment (Example 3)

questions.stem: A university endowment has economic assets of $600 million and economic net worth of $105 million. If the present value of expected future support to the university, an extended liability, rose from $450 million to $500 million with no other changes, economic net worth would most likely:

options.A: Increase by $50 million to $155 million.
options.B: Decrease by $50 million to $55 million.
options.C: Remain unchanged at $105 million.

rationales.A: An increase in a liability decreases net worth rather than increasing it. Economic net worth = economic assets − economic liabilities, so a larger extended liability can only subtract. Net worth of $155 million would require economic assets to rise by $50 million with liabilities unchanged, which is the opposite of what happened here.
rationales.B: Economic net worth = economic assets − economic liabilities. Economic assets are unchanged at $600 million, while the extended liability rises by $500 million − $450 million = $50 million. Economic net worth therefore falls by the same $50 million: $105 million − $50 million = $55 million. The increase in the present value of expected future support consumes almost half of the endowment's original economic net worth, which is why the extended balance sheet view matters for setting the asset allocation.
rationales.C: Extended assets and extended liabilities are both included on the economic balance sheet, and both affect economic net worth; capturing items a conventional balance sheet omits is precisely the purpose of the extended view. The present value of expected future support to the university is an extended liability, so a $50 million increase in it reduces economic net worth from $105 million to $55 million.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Economic Balance Sheet of Auldberg University Endowment (Example 3)

questions.stem: For an institutional investor, an example of an extended portfolio asset is most likely:

options.A: Cash and short-term investments.
options.B: Underground mineral resources.
options.C: Accounts receivable.

rationales.A: Cash and short-term investments are conventional financial assets. They appear on a standard balance sheet and are already captured in a conventional asset allocation, so they are not extended portfolio assets.
rationales.B: Extended portfolio assets are economic resources that a conventional balance sheet omits but that still carry value and risk exposures relevant to asset allocation. For institutional investors, the standard examples are underground mineral resources and the present value of expected future intellectual property royalties. Both should be recognized on the extended economic balance sheet, because an institution holding a large mineral or royalty exposure already has concentrated economic risk that its financial portfolio ought to diversify rather than duplicate.
rationales.C: Accounts receivable owed by clients are conventional financial assets, recognized on a standard balance sheet and already reflected in conventional measures of the institution's assets, so they are not extended portfolio assets.
