drills.los_text: compare the investment objectives of asset-only, liability-relative, and goals-based asset allocation approaches

questions.stem: The three broad approaches to asset allocation are most likely:

options.A: Asset-only, liability-relative, and goals-based.
options.B: Top-down, bottom-up, and hybrid.
options.C: Strategic, tactical, and dynamic.

rationales.A: The three broad approaches to asset allocation are asset-only, liability-relative, and goals-based. An asset-only approach optimizes over the asset side alone; a liability-relative approach models the investor's liabilities explicitly and allocates relative to them; a goals-based approach disaggregates wealth into sub-portfolios matched to individual goals with their own horizons and required probabilities of success.
rationales.B: Top-down, bottom-up, and hybrid describe how research and security selection are organized within a portfolio, not how asset allocation itself is framed, so they are not the three broad approaches.
rationales.C: Strategic, tactical, and dynamic describe horizon and rebalancing distinctions that can be applied within any of the three approaches: a strategic allocation is the long-run policy mix, tactical deviations are short-run departures from it, and dynamic allocation adjusts systematically as conditions change. They are not the approaches themselves.

questions.stem: The typical objective of a mean–variance asset-only approach is most likely:

options.A: To fund liabilities and invest excess assets for growth.
options.B: To achieve goals with specified required probabilities of success.
options.C: To maximize the Sharpe ratio for an acceptable level of volatility.

rationales.A: Funding liabilities first and investing any surplus for growth is the typical objective of a liability-relative approach, used by banks, insurers, and defined benefit pension plans, where the penalty for failing to meet a liability is high.
rationales.B: Achieving goals with specified required probabilities of success is the typical objective of a goals-based approach, applied most often to individual investors whose wealth is divided into sub-portfolios for distinct goals.
rationales.C: The typical objective of an asset-only mean–variance approach is to maximize the Sharpe ratio for an acceptable level of volatility. Because neither liabilities nor goals enter the optimization, the only inputs left are expected returns, volatilities, and correlations, so the best portfolio is the one delivering the highest expected excess return per unit of volatility, subject to the investor's tolerance for total volatility.

questions.stem: A defined benefit pension plan whose primary concern is paying promised benefits at their due dates would most likely adopt which approach?

options.A: Liability-relative.
options.B: Asset-only.
options.C: Purely goals-based.

rationales.A: Defined benefit pension plans, along with banks and insurers, are typical users of the liability-relative approach, because the penalty for failing to meet promised payments on their due dates is high. The allocation is set relative to the characteristics of the liability, hedging its interest rate and inflation sensitivity before any surplus is invested for growth.
rationales.B: An asset-only approach optimizes over the assets without modeling liabilities at all, so it ignores the very obligation that is the plan's primary concern. A portfolio efficient on asset-only terms can still leave benefit payments badly hedged against a fall in discount rates.
rationales.C: A goals-based approach is typically applied to individuals, whose wealth is split into sub-portfolios for goals that differ in horizon and in required probability of success. A defined benefit plan's obligations are contractual liabilities with legally determined due dates rather than personal goals, so the liability-relative approach fits them better.

questions.stem: The investment industry terms LDI and GBI most likely refer, respectively, to:

options.A: Large-diversified investment and global-benchmark investing.
options.B: Liquidity-defined investment and growth-based investing.
options.C: Liability-driven investing and goals-based investing.

rationales.A: Neither expansion is the industry term. LDI stands for liability-driven investing and GBI for goals-based investing; large-diversified investment and global-benchmark investing are not established terms for either approach.
rationales.B: Neither expansion is the industry term. The D in LDI refers to liability-driven, not liquidity-defined, and the G in GBI refers to goals-based, not growth-based; both of these substitutes describe something other than the approach each acronym names.
rationales.C: LDI, liability-driven investing, generally encompasses asset allocation that focuses on funding an investor's liabilities, and is the usual label for the liability-relative approach in practice. GBI, goals-based investing, encompasses asset allocation that focuses on addressing an investor's goals, and is applied most often to individual investors.

questions.stem: A distinction between institutional liabilities and individual goals is most likely that:

options.A: liabilities are legal obligations and goals are not.
options.B: liabilities and goals are functionally identical.
options.C: goals are more predictable than liabilities.

rationales.A: Institutional liabilities are legal obligations: failing to meet them triggers legal and financial consequences for the institution. Individual goals, which express lifestyle or aspirational objectives, carry no such obligation, and failing to meet one does not trigger similar consequences. That difference in legal standing is one of the stated distinctions between the two.
rationales.B: Liabilities and goals are not functionally identical from an investment perspective. Meaningful distinctions separate them, including their legal standing and their predictability, which is why the liability-relative and goals-based approaches are developed as separate frameworks rather than as one.
rationales.C: This reverses the relationship. Institutional liabilities of a given type are numerous and become forecastable through averaging across the group (the law of large numbers), whereas an individual's goals rest on a single case, such as the remaining lifetime of one 65-year-old. Goals are therefore the less predictable of the two.

questions.stem: Individual goals most likely differ from institutional liabilities because individual goals:

options.A: always have a shorter horizon.
options.B: are not subject to averaging across a large group.
options.C: are subject to the law of large numbers.

rationales.A: Individual goals can span horizons from a few months to several decades, from a near-term purchase to a multigenerational bequest. Institutional liabilities range just as widely, so horizon length is not a defining distinction between the two.
rationales.B: Institutional liabilities of a given type, such as pension benefits, are numerous, and averaging across the group makes them forecastable. An individual's goals rest on a single case, for example a 65-year-old's remaining life, and so are not subject to the law of large numbers. That absence of averaging is what makes individual goals less predictable than institutional liabilities.
rationales.C: This is exactly backwards. It is institutional liabilities, pooled across many participants or claimants, that benefit from averaging; the goals of a single individual do not.

questions.stem: The goals-based approach to asset allocation is most likely used by:

options.A: a defined benefit pension plan.
options.B: a large commercial bank.
options.C: an individual investor.

rationales.A: A defined benefit pension plan has a contractual benefit stream to fund, so it typically adopts a liability-relative approach, matching the size, interest rate sensitivity, and inflation sensitivity of the assets to that of the obligation rather than to lifestyle or aspirational goals.
rationales.B: A large commercial bank manages its assets against deposits and other obligations and so also applies a liability-relative approach, not a goals-based one.
rationales.C: Goals-based asset allocation is used primarily for individuals and families. Wealth is divided into sub-portfolios aligned with distinct lifestyle and aspirational goals, each with its own time horizon and its own required probability of success, which is why the individual investor is the typical user.

drills.los_text: contrast concepts of risk relevant to asset-only, liability-relative, and goals-based asset allocation approaches

questions.stem: In the baseline asset-only mean–variance approach, the primary risk measure is most likely:

options.A: the shortfall risk relative to liabilities.
options.B: the maximum probability of failing to achieve a goal.
options.C: the volatility of portfolio return.

rationales.A: Shortfall relative to a liability is the risk measure of the liability-relative approach, which compares asset value with the value of the obligations rather than looking at the assets in isolation.
rationales.B: The maximum probability of failing to achieve a goal is the goals-based risk measure; risk limits in that framework are expressed as a tolerable chance of missing each individual goal.
rationales.C: The baseline asset-only approach, mean-variance optimization, uses the volatility (standard deviation) of portfolio return as its primary measure of risk. Because the approach considers the assets on their own, it has neither a liability nor a goal against which a shortfall could be measured.

questions.stem: Risk in a liability-relative approach is most likely underpinned by:

options.A: differences between asset and liability characteristics.
options.B: the volatility of individual asset class returns.
options.C: the probability of falling short of a goal.

rationales.A: Risk in a liability-relative context is generally underpinned by the differences between asset and liability characteristics: their relative size, their interest rate sensitivity, and their sensitivity to inflation. A mismatch in any of those three moves the surplus and the funded ratio, which is what the approach is built to control.
rationales.B: The volatility of individual asset class returns, taken in isolation, is the asset-only view of risk. It leaves the liability side out of the analysis altogether and so cannot capture a size, duration, or inflation mismatch.
rationales.C: The probability of falling short of an individual goal sub-portfolio is the goals-based framing of risk, not the liability-relative one.

questions.stem: In a goals-based approach, risk limits are most likely quantified as:

options.A: the maximum acceptable duration mismatch.
options.B: the maximum acceptable portfolio standard deviation.
options.C: the maximum acceptable probability of missing a goal.

rationales.A: A maximum acceptable duration mismatch between assets and liabilities is a liability-relative risk limit: it constrains how far the interest rate sensitivity of the assets may drift from that of the obligations.
rationales.B: A cap on portfolio-level standard deviation is an asset-only risk limit, taken from mean-variance optimization. It says nothing about whether any particular goal is met.
rationales.C: In a goals-based approach each goal is funded by its own sub-portfolio and carries a required probability of success, so the risk limit is stated as the maximum acceptable probability of not achieving that goal.

questions.stem: The risk measures that a mean-variance asset allocation can incorporate are most likely:

options.A: only tail risk measures, such as value at risk and drawdown.
options.B: tracking risk and downside risk measures.
options.C: volatility only.

rationales.A: A mean-variance asset allocation is not limited to tail risk. Value at risk and peak-to-trough maximum drawdown can indeed be brought in, but so can tracking risk relative to a benchmark and semi-variance, so a tail-only list is too narrow.
rationales.B: A mean-variance asset allocation can incorporate risk sensitivities beyond return volatility, including tracking risk measured relative to a benchmark and downside risk represented by semi-variance, peak-to-trough maximum drawdown, and value at risk.
rationales.C: Although the optimization itself is variance-based, the resulting allocation can be evaluated and constrained with additional measures. Volatility is the baseline risk measure of the approach, not the only one it can accommodate.

questions.stem: Volatility of the funded ratio, the ratio of asset value to liability value, is most likely a risk concept of the approach known as:

options.A: liability-relative.
options.B: asset-only.
options.C: goals-based.

rationales.A: The funded ratio sets asset value against liability value, so its volatility measures how far the assets may drift from the obligations they support. Volatility of the funded ratio is a liability-relative risk concept, alongside surplus volatility.
rationales.B: An asset-only approach carries no liability in the analysis, so no funded ratio can be formed; its risk concept is the volatility of portfolio return.
rationales.C: A goals-based approach measures risk as the probability of not achieving each goal rather than through a funded ratio.

questions.stem: Standard deviation of returns most likely:

options.A: is meaningful only for normally distributed returns.
options.B: is used exclusively in asset-only approaches.
options.C: can be applied in all three approaches.

rationales.A: The usefulness of standard deviation is not conditioned on an assumption of normally distributed returns; it is presented as a general statistical measure of dispersion.
rationales.B: Standard deviation is not exclusive to asset-only work. A given statistical risk measure may be relevant in any of the three approaches to asset allocation.
rationales.C: A given statistical risk measure may be relevant in any of the three approaches. Standard deviation can be used to assess overall portfolio volatility, which is the asset-only application, and also surplus volatility or funded ratio volatility, which are liability-relative applications, so it is not confined to one framework.

questions.stem: In a goals-based framework, overall portfolio risk is most likely structured as:

options.A: the correlation among sub-portfolios.
options.B: the weighted sum of the risks of each goal.
options.C: the volatility of the aggregate portfolio return.

rationales.A: Correlation among the goal sub-portfolios is a technical detail of how the sub-portfolios combine, not the way overall risk is framed in a goals-based approach.
rationales.B: In goals-based approaches, overall portfolio risk is the weighted sum of the risks associated with each goal. Structuring risk that way underscores that the risks relate to multiple future points in time, one for each goal, rather than to a single portfolio horizon.
rationales.C: Volatility of the aggregate portfolio return is the asset-only conception of overall risk; it collapses the separate goals and their differing horizons into one number.

drills.los_text: explain how asset classes are used to represent exposures to systematic risk and discuss criteria for asset class specification

questions.stem: The three asset "super classes" identified by Greer (1997) are most likely:

options.A: Domestic, international, and emerging market assets.
options.B: Capital, consumable/transformable, and store of value assets.
options.C: Equities, fixed income, and alternatives.

rationales.A: This is a geographic segmentation of a portfolio rather than Greer's typology. Greer classifies assets by the economic source of their value, not by the domicile of the issuer, so the same security could sit in any of these three buckets without its super class changing.
rationales.B: Greer's three super classes are capital assets, which are an ongoing source of value and can therefore be valued by discounting expected future cash flows; consumable/transformable assets, such as commodities, which are consumed or converted into something else and generate no ongoing income stream; and store of value assets, such as currencies and art, which are neither consumed nor income-producing but hold value instead.
rationales.C: This is a conventional practitioner asset class listing rather than a set of super classes. Equities and fixed income both sit inside the single super class of capital assets, since each is an ongoing source of value that can be valued by discounting expected cash flows.

questions.stem: The criteria for effectively specifying asset classes least likely require that:

options.A: assets within an asset class be relatively homogeneous.
options.B: asset classes have similar historical returns.
options.C: asset classes be mutually exclusive.

rationales.A: Homogeneity within an asset class is the first criterion. A class whose members are not similar to one another cannot be described by a single set of risk and return forecasts, so the inputs handed to the optimizer would not represent what is actually held.
rationales.B: Similar historical returns across classes is not one of the criteria, and choosing classes because their past returns resemble each other would work against the purpose of allocation. The five criteria are that assets within a class be relatively homogeneous; that classes be mutually exclusive; that they be diversifying; that as a group they make up a preponderance of world investable wealth; and that each have the capacity to absorb a meaningful allocation without affecting the portfolio's liquidity or transaction costs.
rationales.C: Mutual exclusivity is the second criterion. Overlapping classes double-count the same exposures, which inflates the apparent breadth of the opportunity set and makes the correlation and risk estimates used in optimization unreliable.

questions.stem: The pairwise correlation above which an included asset class is generally considered non-diversifying is closest to:

rationales.A: A pairwise correlation above roughly 0.95, estimated from enough observations to give confidence in the estimate, is generally undesirable. An asset class that moves that closely with one already in the opportunity set is effectively redundant: it adds no diversification while still consuming governance attention, manager research, and transaction costs.
rationales.B: This is not the threshold used. A pairwise correlation of 0.75 still leaves a substantial share of each class's variation independent of the other, so two classes at this level would normally be retained separately as genuinely diversifying.
rationales.C: This is not the threshold used. A correlation of 0.50 is only moderate, and classes that co-move this loosely are clearly diversifying rather than redundant; setting the bar here would strip the opportunity set of classes that are doing useful work.

questions.stem: For a US investor, defining both "global equities" and "US equities" as asset classes most likely violates the criterion of:

options.A: capacity to absorb a meaningful allocation.
options.B: homogeneity within an asset class.
options.C: mutual exclusivity of asset classes.

rationales.A: Capacity concerns whether a class is large and liquid enough to absorb a meaningful share of the investor's portfolio without moving prices or driving up transaction costs. It is a question about the scale of the class relative to the investor, not about overlap between two classes, and both global and US equities are easily large enough to pass it.
rationales.B: Homogeneity concerns whether the holdings inside a single class are similar enough to share one set of risk and return forecasts. Global equities are reasonably homogeneous taken on their own; the defect here lies in the relationship between the two classes rather than within either of them.
rationales.C: Global equities already contain US equities, so the two classes overlap and the same securities are counted twice in the opportunity set. If US domestic common equities is defined as one class, then world equities ex-US is the appropriate companion rather than global equities. Overlap of this kind violates mutual exclusivity and corrupts the correlation and risk inputs used in the allocation.

questions.stem: Hedge fund strategies are most likely distinguished from asset classes because they:

options.A: cannot be given a percentage allocation.
options.B: have higher expected returns than any asset class.
options.C: lack an inherent, non-skill-based expected return premium.

rationales.A: Strategies can be and routinely are assigned percentage allocations in the same way true asset classes are, so allocability is not what separates the two. The distinction lies in where the expected return comes from, not in whether a weight can be placed on the line item.
rationales.B: A high expected return is not the defining distinction. Many strategies are expected to earn less than equities, and a high expected return does not disqualify something from being an asset class; what matters is whether the premium arises from the exposure itself or from the manager.
rationales.C: An asset class generally offers an inherent, non-skill-based ex ante expected return premium: holding the exposure is expected to be rewarded regardless of who holds it. A strategy instead applies skill to investments drawn from underlying asset classes, so its expected return depends on the manager rather than on the exposure, which is why it is treated as a way of accessing risk rather than as a distinct source of it.

questions.stem: Excessive asset class granularity is most likely problematic because:

options.A: sub-asset classes offer higher returns than broad asset classes.
options.B: sub-asset classes share common risk factors and correlate highly.
options.C: sub-asset classes lack sufficient history for optimization.

rationales.A: Finer segmentation does not raise expected returns. Sub-asset classes are subsets of the broad classes, so in aggregate they earn what the broad class earns, less the additional costs of researching, implementing, and rebalancing a larger number of line items.
rationales.B: At the sub-asset class level, many of the same underlying risk factors drive returns, which produces substantially positive correlations among the segments. The more granular the segmentation, the less distinctive each piece becomes, so the optimizer is handed inputs it cannot reliably distinguish between while governance and rebalancing burdens rise. Broad asset classes overlap far less in their sources of risk and so remain genuinely diversifying with respect to one another.
rationales.C: Thin return history is a real practical difficulty for some narrow segments, but it is a secondary concern rather than the central objection, and many sub-asset classes do have long series available. The primary problem is the loss of distinctiveness that follows from shared risk factors.

questions.stem: In current professional practice, a common top-level asset class listing most likely comprises:

options.A: Global public equity, global private equity, global fixed income, and real assets.
options.B: Large-cap, small-cap, and mid-cap equity.
options.C: Domestic bonds, international bonds, and cash.

rationales.A: Global public equity, global private equity, global fixed income, and real assets are the four groupings that most commonly appear at the top level in current practice. Between them they represent a preponderance of world investable wealth, they are mutually exclusive, each is diversifying with respect to the others, and each is large enough to absorb a meaningful allocation.
rationales.B: These are capitalization segments within a single asset class rather than a top-level listing. They share most of their underlying risk factors and so correlate highly with one another, failing the diversification criterion, and the listing leaves fixed income, private equity, and real assets entirely unrepresented.
rationales.C: This listing omits public equity, private equity, and real assets, so it covers only a small part of world investable wealth and cannot serve as the opportunity set for a strategic asset allocation.

questions.stem: Pairwise correlations considered in isolation are most likely to:

options.A: fully capture an asset's diversification value.
options.B: overstate an asset's diversification value.
options.C: mismeasure an asset's diversification value.

rationales.A: A pairwise correlation compares one asset with one other asset, so it cannot see how the asset relates to the rest of the portfolio taken together. An asset can be an exact weighted combination of two assets already held, adding no diversification value whatsoever, and still show only moderate correlation with each of them individually.
rationales.B: The error is not directional. Pairwise correlations can make a redundant asset appear diversifying, but they can equally understate an asset whose contribution shows up only in combination with other holdings, so they do not systematically overstate the benefit.
rationales.C: Because a pairwise measure ignores an asset's relationship to the portfolio as a whole, judging diversification value from it alone supports limited or incorrect conclusions. An asset that is an exact weighted combination of two existing holdings adds nothing to the portfolio, yet its pairwise correlations with each of those two can be only moderate and so look attractive. Measures that use the full covariance structure, such as the asset's marginal contribution to portfolio risk, are needed instead.

drills.los_text: explain the use of risk factors in asset allocation and their relation to traditional asset class–based approaches

questions.stem: A factor-based asset allocation approach most likely differs from a traditional asset class-based approach in that:

options.A: factor-based approaches produce superior outcomes.
options.B: factor-based approaches cannot be mapped into asset class space.
options.C: factor-based approaches begin with risk factors as the unit of analysis.

rationales.A: Adopting a factor-based approach does not by default lead to superior outcomes. The set of achievable portfolios is technically the same as under an asset class approach, because the factor exposures are ultimately expressed through the same underlying investments; what changes is the lens used to specify and monitor risk, not the opportunity set.
rationales.B: A chosen set of risk exposures in factor space can be mapped back into asset class space for implementation, since positions must eventually be taken in investable assets. The two representations describe the same portfolio from different angles.
rationales.C: In a factor-based approach one begins by specifying the risk factors and the desired exposure to each, and asset classes are then described in terms of their sensitivities to those factors. In a traditional approach the asset class itself is the unit of analysis and the optimization runs directly over classes.

questions.stem: Risk factors most likely differ from asset classes in that risk factors:

options.A: have universally accepted definitions.
options.B: are directly investable in cash markets.
options.C: require long and short positions in assets.

rationales.A: Factor definitions are not standardized. Value, momentum, size, and quality are each constructed differently from one implementation to the next, and the resulting exposures are estimated with error. Membership in an asset class, by contrast, is comparatively unambiguous.
rationales.B: Risk factors are generally not directly investable. A factor is a source of return common to many securities rather than a security in its own right, so no cash market instrument delivers the factor on its own.
rationales.C: Because factors are not directly investable, isolating one generally requires offsetting long and short positions in assets. Such a spread position strips out the exposures the investor does not want and leaves the factor and its associated expected return premium. An asset class, by contrast, can simply be bought long.

questions.stem: A factor exposure to inflation is most likely isolated by:

options.A: Long nominal Treasuries, short inflation-linked bonds.
options.B: Long VIX futures.
options.C: Long inflation-linked bonds, short nominal Treasuries.

rationales.A: The standard factor representation for inflation is a long position in nominal Treasuries against a short position in inflation-linked bonds. The two legs share real-rate and term exposure, which the pairing cancels, leaving only the component that distinguishes them: the compensation for inflation.
rationales.B: VIX futures are a proxy for implied equity volatility, not for inflation. They isolate a volatility factor and leave the inflation component untouched.
rationales.C: This pairing is the reverse of the standard inflation representation. Long inflation-linked bonds against short nominal Treasuries isolates the opposite exposure to the one sought.

questions.stem: A credit spread factor exposure is most likely isolated by:

options.A: Long high-quality credit, short Treasuries.
options.B: Long 10+ year Treasuries, short 1–3 year Treasuries.
options.C: Long inflation-linked bonds, short nominal bonds.

rationales.A: The credit spread factor is represented by a long position in high-quality credit against a short position in Treasuries or other government bonds. Both legs carry broadly similar duration and real-rate exposure, so the pairing nets out interest rate risk and leaves the spread of corporate over government yields, which is the credit component.
rationales.B: A long position in 10+ year Treasuries against a short position in 1–3 year Treasuries is a term-structure trade. Both legs are government credit, so what remains after the pairing is duration exposure, not credit spread.
rationales.C: A long position in inflation-linked bonds against a short position in nominal bonds isolates inflation exposure, because the two legs differ in their inflation linkage rather than in credit quality.

questions.stem: Interest in using factors rather than asset classes for asset allocation is least likely motivated by:

options.A: Recognition that highly correlated asset classes belong in one class.
options.B: Evidence that factor approaches always raise risk-adjusted returns.
options.C: A desire to shape allocation around goals asset classes cannot express.

rationales.A: Acknowledging that asset classes with high pairwise correlations are better defined as parts of the same high-level asset class is one of the stated considerations. Apparent diversification across such classes is not genuine diversification, and a factor lens exposes that.
rationales.B: Adopting a factor-based asset allocation approach does not, by default, lead to superior investment outcomes. Nothing supports a claim that factor-based approaches always yield higher risk-adjusted returns, so this is not one of the considerations behind the interest in factors.
rationales.C: The desire to shape an asset allocation around goals that cannot be expressed in terms of asset classes is one of the stated considerations.

questions.stem: Modeling asset allocation using asset classes as the unit of analysis most likely:

options.A: Precludes outcomes that factor-based approaches can achieve.
options.B: Obscures sensitivity to overlapping risk factors such as inflation.
options.C: Reveals cross-asset factor overlaps such as inflation risk.

rationales.A: Technically the set of achievable investment outcomes is the same, all else equal. Asset-class and factor-based approaches span the same opportunity set, so neither is theoretically barred from reaching the outcomes of the other. The difference between them lies in visibility and control of risk exposures, not in what is attainable.
rationales.B: Modeling asset allocation with asset classes as the unit of analysis tends to obscure the portfolio's sensitivity to overlapping risk factors, such as inflation risk, because a single factor is embedded in several classes at once. Controlling risk exposures may then be problematic.
rationales.C: This reverses the point. Asset-class modeling hides rather than reveals cross-asset factor overlaps; explicit visibility into those overlapping exposures is what a factor-based approach supplies.

questions.stem: A factor-based approach to asset allocation most likely addresses the concern that:

options.A: Some asset classes lack a market-cap-weighted proxy.
options.B: Equity risk dominates a seemingly well-diversified portfolio.
options.C: Factor-based approaches guarantee superior returns.

rationales.A: The absence of a market-cap-weighted proxy for some asset classes is a separate implementation issue, about how a class is represented in a portfolio, rather than a concern that motivates factor-based modeling.
rationales.B: One motivation for factor-based approaches is the realization that equity risk can be the dominant risk exposure even in a seemingly well-diversified portfolio, because many of the asset classes held load on the same equity factor. A factor lens makes that concentration visible.
rationales.C: No guarantee of superior returns is on offer. A factor-based approach does not, by default, lead to better investment outcomes, so this is not a concern that the approach addresses.

drills.los_text: recommend and justify an asset allocation based on an investor's objectives and constraints

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth fund quantifies its risk tolerance as a willingness to bear portfolio volatility of up to 17% per year, tied to an unwillingness to let the fund fall below 90% funded. Among the candidate allocations, Mix B has the highest expected return, 8.88%, with volatility of 16.63%, a 5% VaR of −18.48%, and a Sharpe ratio of 0.353, below that of Mix A. Mix B most likely:

options.A: Does not merit further consideration.
options.B: Should be preferred for its higher expected return.
options.C: Must be rejected for violating the volatility tolerance.

rationales.A: Mix B does offer the highest expected return, and its volatility sits inside the stated tolerance, but its Sharpe ratio of 0.353 is lower than Mix A's. That tells the fund the additional risk Mix B takes on is used inefficiently: the extra expected return does not compensate for the extra volatility. On that basis Mix B does not deserve additional consideration.
rationales.B: Choosing on expected return alone ignores risk-adjusted performance and the fund's other constraints. Mix B's higher expected return is bought with risk that its lower Sharpe ratio shows to be inefficiently deployed.
rationales.C: Mix B's volatility of 16.63% per year is below the 17% the fund is willing to bear, so the volatility constraint is not violated and rejection on that ground would be wrong. The weakness of Mix B is its Sharpe ratio, not its volatility.

questions.curriculum_ref: Strategic Asset Allocation: Asset Only (GPFC case)

questions.stem: Under utility theory, the optimal asset allocation is most likely the one that:

options.A: Minimizes the variance of wealth at the investment horizon.
options.B: Maximizes expected utility at the horizon, subject to weight constraints.
options.C: Maximizes expected wealth at the investment horizon.

rationales.A: Pure variance minimization ignores return. An investor who only minimized the variance of terminal wealth would hold the least volatile portfolio available regardless of what it earns. Utility theory instead trades expected return off against risk.
rationales.B: Under utility theory the optimal asset allocation is the one expected to provide the highest utility to the investor at the investment horizon, subject to the constraint that the weights sum to 1 and to any other constraints on the weights. Because the utility function embeds the investor's risk aversion, the maximization balances expected return against risk rather than optimizing either one alone.
rationales.C: Maximizing expected wealth ignores risk aversion. It would push the investor into the highest-returning asset irrespective of its volatility, which the risk-aversion term in the utility function rules out.

questions.stem: In the simplest asset allocation, with one risky asset and one risk-free asset, mean–variance utility implies that the optimal weight in the risky asset most likely:

options.A: Rises with both risk aversion and variance.
options.B: Varies with excess return per unit of volatility, independent of risk aversion.
options.C: Falls with risk aversion and rises with excess return per unit of variance.

rationales.A: This has risk aversion multiplied rather than divided and volatility multiplied rather than divided, giving w* = λ × (μ − rf) × σ². The correct expression is w* = (1/λ) × (μ − rf)/σ², so a more risk-averse investor (higher λ) and a more volatile risky asset (higher σ²) each reduce the optimal allocation rather than increase it.
rationales.B: This formulation leaves risk aversion out altogether and mishandles variance, scaling by volatility instead, as in w* = (μ − rf) × σ. The optimal weight divides the risk premium by variance and by the risk aversion coefficient, so an allocation that does not depend on λ cannot be optimal under mean–variance utility.
rationales.C: The optimal weight is w* = (1/λ) × (μ − rf)/σ², where λ is the risk aversion coefficient, μ − rf the risky asset's expected excess return over the risk-free rate, and σ² its variance. The allocation to the risky asset is therefore inversely proportional to risk aversion and directly proportional to the risky asset's expected excess return per unit of variance.

questions.curriculum_ref: Optimal Choice in the Simplest Case (sidebar)

questions.stem: In selecting a strategic asset allocation, the step that most likely involves conducting simulations to test the sensitivity of outcomes to changes in capital market expectations is:

options.A: Testing the robustness of potential choices.
options.B: Determining risk tolerance.
options.C: Developing a range of potential allocation choices.

rationales.A: Testing the robustness of potential choices is Step 8 of the nine-step process. It often involves conducting simulations to evaluate potential results and to test the sensitivity of outcomes to changes in capital market expectations, since the return and risk estimates feeding an optimization are themselves uncertain.
rationales.B: Determining risk tolerance is Step 2. It quantifies the investor's willingness and ability to bear risk, for instance as a volatility or shortfall limit, rather than simulating outcomes.
rationales.C: Developing a range of potential asset allocation choices for consideration is Step 7. It relies on optimization exercises to generate the candidate mixes; the sensitivity testing of those candidates comes afterward.

questions.stem: A frozen defined benefit pension plan is choosing between a mean–variance efficient mix of 65% equities and 35% fixed income and a mix of 10% equities and 90% liability-hedging fixed income. The liability-hedging mix is most likely preferred because it:

options.A: Maximizes the Sharpe ratio.
options.B: Offers the higher expected return.
options.C: Defeases the liabilities, removing meaningful risk of further contributions.

rationales.A: The mean–variance efficient 65/35 mix is the one that likely has the higher Sharpe ratio, and the liability-hedging mix is chosen despite that, not because of it. Sharpe ratio maximization is the wrong objective for a frozen plan whose purpose is to discharge a fixed set of liabilities.
rationales.B: The 10% equity, 90% liability-hedging mix has a considerably lower expected return and sits below the efficient frontier. Expected return is what it gives up, not what recommends it.
rationales.C: With roughly $1.125 billion of fixed income whose risk characteristics are closely matched to about $1.087 billion of pension liabilities, the portfolio covers the liabilities with a buffer, so the liabilities are defeased. The sponsor should then face no meaningful risk of having to make further contributions, which is an excellent outcome for both sponsor and pensioners and worth more to a frozen plan than the extra expected return of the efficient mix.

questions.curriculum_ref: Strategic Asset Allocation: Liability Relative (GPLE case)

questions.stem: A liability glide path is most likely particularly relevant for:

options.A: Overfunded pension plans.
options.B: Underfunded pension plans.
options.C: Sovereign wealth funds.

rationales.A: An overfunded plan already holds a surplus, so raising the funded status is not the pressing objective and the need to de-risk along a pre-set schedule is far less acute. A glide path can still be used to lock in a surplus, but it is not the setting the technique is designed around.
rationales.B: The liability glide path technique is particularly relevant to underfunded pension plans. The objective is to increase the funded status over time while reducing surplus risk: the plan begins with a return-seeking allocation large enough to close the funding gap, and as the funded ratio improves it shifts progressively into liability-hedging assets (long duration bonds, LDI overlays). The schedule is specified in advance and keyed to funded status, so risk comes out of the portfolio exactly as the plan can afford to give up return.
rationales.C: A sovereign wealth fund is generally an asset-only investor. With no contractual liability stream and no funding gap to close, there is no funded status to glide along, so the technique does not apply in its usual form.

questions.stem: Allocation A holds 40% cash, 50% bonds, and 10% equities. Allocation B holds 10% cash, 30% bonds, 45% equities, and 15% diversifying assets. Under a goals-based approach, Allocation A is most likely appropriate for:

options.A: Short-term lifestyle and education goals.
options.B: Long-horizon aspirational goals.
options.C: Long-horizon goals with a high required success probability.

rationales.A: Allocation A stresses liquidity and stability: 90% of it sits in cash and bonds and only 10% in equities. That profile suits goals that are close at hand and whose shortfall would be felt immediately, which is exactly the character of short-term lifestyle spending and near-term education funding. In goals-based asset allocation each goal gets its own sub-portfolio, and the sub-portfolio for a short-horizon, high-required-probability goal is dominated by low-volatility assets so the money is there when the goal comes due.
rationales.B: An aspirational goal decades away, such as a large charitable gift, has both the time to recover from drawdowns and a lower required probability of success. It therefore warrants a growth-oriented sub-portfolio like Allocation B, with 45% equities and 15% diversifying assets; holding 40% cash against a goal that far out would almost guarantee a real-terms shortfall.
rationales.C: A long horizon combined with a high required probability of success, as with a special-needs trust, favors a moderately growth-oriented allocation like Allocation B rather than Allocation A. The long horizon means the assets must outgrow inflation over decades, and the diversifying sleeve plus the bond allocation in B supply the stability the high required probability demands; Allocation A would protect the near term at the cost of the goal itself.

questions.stem: Goals-based asset allocation most likely helps investors accept more-optimal portfolios by:

options.A: Prohibiting risky assets in every sub-portfolio.
options.B: Placing higher-risk assets in long-horizon aspirational sub-portfolios.
options.C: Combining all goals into a single aggregate optimization.

rationales.A: The approach embraces appropriately placed risky assets rather than prohibiting them. A blanket ban would push every sub-portfolio toward cash and bonds and would leave long-dated goals underfunded in real terms, which is the opposite of the behavioral benefit being described.
rationales.B: Goals-based asset allocation may help investors embrace more-optimal portfolios by adding higher-risk assets, which without context might frighten the investor, to longer-term aspirational sub-portfolios, while adopting a more conservative allocation for lifestyle-preservation sub-portfolios. Labeling each sub-portfolio by the goal it funds gives the risky holdings a context the investor can accept: the volatility is attached to a goal decades away and with a low required probability of success, not to the money that pays next year's bills.
rationales.C: The strength of goals-based asset allocation is disaggregation, not aggregation. Pooling every goal into one optimization is the traditional approach; it loses the goal-by-goal horizon and required-probability information that makes the investor comfortable holding risk in the first place.

drills.los_text: describe the use of the global market portfolio as a baseline portfolio in asset allocation

questions.stem: Financial theory most likely supports the global market portfolio as a baseline for asset allocation because it:

options.A: eliminates all forms of investment risk.
options.B: minimizes diversifiable, uncompensated risk.
options.C: produces the highest expected return across markets.

rationales.A: Diversification removes only the idiosyncratic component of risk. The global market portfolio still carries full systematic risk, which is compensated and cannot be diversified away; a portfolio free of all risk would be the risk-free asset, not the market.
rationales.B: Financial theory suggests investors should consider the global market-value-weighted portfolio of all investable assets as the baseline asset allocation. Holding every asset in proportion to its market value minimizes diversifiable risk, which in principle is uncompensated, and the resulting weights reflect the balancing of supply and demand across world markets, so they embody the collective pricing judgment of all investors. Deviating from that baseline is a deliberate active decision that should be justified.
rationales.C: The global market portfolio maximizes diversification, not raw expected return. A portfolio concentrated in the highest-expected-return assets would have a higher expected return and a worse risk-adjusted profile; the baseline is defended on efficiency grounds, not on level of return.

questions.stem: The theoretical support for the global market portfolio as a baseline most likely comes from:

options.A: Modigliani–Miller theorems.
options.B: The efficient market hypothesis.
options.C: The two-fund separation theorem.

rationales.A: The Modigliani–Miller theorems concern corporate capital structure and the irrelevance of financing mix to firm value. They say nothing about how an investor should combine risky assets, so they offer no support for a market-value-weighted baseline.
rationales.B: The efficient market hypothesis concerns how quickly prices incorporate information, that is, pricing efficiency. It implies active management is difficult, but it does not by itself specify the composition of the optimal risky portfolio.
rationales.C: The two-fund separation theorem provides the support: all investors optimally hold some combination of a single risk-free asset and one optimal portfolio of all risky assets. Because every investor holds that same risky portfolio, in equilibrium it must be the market portfolio, which globally is the global market value-weighted portfolio. Investors then differ only in how much they put in the risk-free asset, which is where risk tolerance enters.

questions.stem: The global market portfolio is constructed in two phases. The first phase most likely involves:

options.A: Selecting individual securities within each country.
options.B: Allocating across global stocks, bonds, and real assets.
options.C: Tilting toward the investor's home-country market.

rationales.A: Individual security selection is not phase 1. Security-level weights come in phase 2, and even then they are set mechanically by capitalization rather than chosen name by name.
rationales.B: Phase 1 allocates assets in proportion to the global portfolio of stocks, bonds, and real assets, that is, the split across the broad asset classes. Phase 2 then disaggregates each broad asset class into regional, country, and ultimately security weights, again using capitalization weights, so the whole portfolio is market-value weighted from the top down.
rationales.C: Home-country tilting is a deliberate departure from the baseline, not a step in building it. The construction described is entirely market-value weighted and carries no preference for the investor's domestic market.

questions.stem: Home-country bias in asset allocation is most likely:

options.A: Desirable and encouraged by financial theory.
options.B: Rare and limited to small emerging markets.
options.C: Common in markets of all sizes, including the US and eurozone.

rationales.A: Theory points to the global market-value-weighted portfolio as the baseline, so overweighting the domestic market is a departure from it and must be justified on other grounds, such as liabilities denominated in the home currency, taxes, or a currency-risk preference. It is not something theory encourages.
rationales.B: Home-country bias is widespread rather than rare, and it is not a feature only of small or less developed markets. Investors in the largest and most liquid markets display it too, so confining it to small emerging markets understates it badly.
rationales.C: The favoring of domestic over non-domestic investment relative to global market-value weights, known as home-country bias, is very common. It appears in relatively small economies, where the domestic market is a tiny fraction of global market value, and equally in very large markets such as the US and the eurozone. Its prevalence is one reason practitioners treat the global market portfolio as a starting point rather than a description of how portfolios are actually held.

questions.stem: Common tilts away from the global market portfolio most likely include:

options.A: Growth, large cap, and developed markets.
options.B: Cash, government bonds, and short duration.
options.C: Value, small cap, and emerging markets.

rationales.A: Growth and large-cap tilts are not the common tilts observed. They point in the opposite direction from the value and size tilts investors actually take, and a developed-markets-only stance is the reverse of the emerging markets overweight.
rationales.B: A cash, government bond, and short duration stance describes a conservative or defensive posture, not a tilt away from global market-value weights in the sense meant here. These are not the common biases identified.
rationales.C: The common tilts away from the global market portfolio are overweighting the home-country market, value, size in the form of small cap, and emerging markets. The value and size tilts are the long-documented style premiums, while the emerging markets tilt reflects a view that their growth or risk premium is not fully captured by current market-value weights. Each is an active decision for which the investor should be able to articulate a justification.

questions.stem: One practical limitation of using the global market portfolio as a baseline is most likely that:

options.A: market-cap weights are unstable and change daily.
options.B: the portfolio holds too few asset classes to be well diversified.
options.C: private real estate and private equity are not divisible into small pieces.

rationales.A: Market-value weights do move with prices, but they drift gradually and a cap-weighted portfolio rebalances itself as prices change. That is an administrative detail rather than a fundamental limitation on using the global market portfolio as a baseline.
rationales.B: The global market portfolio is highly diversified by construction: it holds every investable asset in proportion to its market value, across asset classes, regions, and countries. Too few asset classes is the opposite of its defining feature.
rationales.C: Private commercial real estate and global private equity assets are not easily carved into pieces of a size accessible to most investors, which is a genuine practical limitation. The theoretical global market portfolio includes these non-traded assets, but an individual investor cannot buy a proportionate slice of them. Practically, proxies for the global market portfolio are therefore often based only on traded assets, which means the baseline actually used is not the one theory describes.

questions.stem: Alternative weighting schemes to market-cap weighting for the global market portfolio most likely include:

options.A: GDP weighting or equal weighting.
options.B: Trailing-earnings weighting.
options.C: Book-value weighting.

rationales.A: Alternative weighting schemes some investors implement include GDP weight and equal weight. GDP weighting ties exposure to the size of each economy rather than the size of its listed market, which lifts weights in economies whose equity markets are small relative to output; equal weighting removes the cap-weighted tilt toward the largest issuers. Either is a defensible choice, but it is a deviation from cap weighting, and it is useful discipline to articulate a justification for any such deviation.
rationales.B: Weighting by trailing earnings is not among the alternatives identified. It is a fundamental-indexation idea rather than one of the recognized substitutes for market-value weighting at the global asset allocation level.
rationales.C: Weighting by book value is likewise not the identified alternative. Like earnings weighting it is an accounting-based measure of size and would introduce a value tilt as a by-product rather than serve as a clean baseline.

drills.los_text: discuss strategic implementation choices in asset allocation, including passive/active choices and vehicles for implementing passive and active mandates

questions.stem: The passive/active choice in implementing an asset allocation applies along two dimensions. These dimensions are most likely:

options.A: Cost minimization and risk minimization.
options.B: Deviation from the strategic allocation and implementation within each asset class.
options.C: Domestic versus international and active versus passive.

rationales.A: Cost and risk minimization are considerations that arise within each dimension rather than dimensions in their own right. Every passive/active decision, whether to deviate from the strategic allocation and how to invest within an asset class, trades expected value added against cost and tracking risk, so cost and risk sit one level below the framing.
rationales.B: The two dimensions are, first, management of the strategic asset allocation itself, meaning whether to deviate from it tactically or dynamically rather than hold the policy weights, and second, the passive/active choice in investing the allocation within a given asset class, such as indexing an equity sleeve versus funding an active manager in it. The two decisions are made separately, so a portfolio can be active on one dimension and passive on the other.
rationales.C: Geographic scope is an asset-class and opportunity-set decision, not a dimension of the passive/active choice, and "active versus passive" restates the choice itself rather than naming a dimension along which it is made.

questions.stem: Tactical asset allocation is best described as:

options.A: Deliberate short-term deviations from the strategic asset allocation.
options.B: Long-term deviations driven by changes in fundamental views.
options.C: Revisions driven by changes in the investor's circumstances or IPS.

rationales.A: Tactical asset allocation involves deliberate short-term deviations from the strategic asset allocation, taken to reflect short-term capital market views, for example to exploit a perceived deviation of an asset class from its equilibrium value. The strategic allocation itself stays in place; the tactical position is a temporary overlay on it that is expected to be unwound as the perceived mispricing closes.
rationales.B: Deviations motivated by longer-term valuation signals or economic views describe dynamic asset allocation, not tactical asset allocation. Both are intentional departures from the policy weights, so what separates them is the horizon of the view behind the deviation, not whether the deviation is deliberate.
rationales.C: A change in the investor's circumstances or in the investment policy statement calls for revising the strategic asset allocation itself, since the objectives and constraints the allocation was built to meet have changed. Tactical asset allocation takes the strategic allocation as given and deviates from it temporarily.

questions.curriculum_ref: Passive/Active Management of Asset Class Weights

questions.stem: Dynamic asset allocation most likely differs from tactical asset allocation in that dynamic asset allocation:

options.A: Involves purely random deviations from the strategic allocation.
options.B: Reflects deviations motivated by longer-term valuation or economic views.
options.C: Is based on shorter-term views.

rationales.A: Both approaches involve intentional, view-driven deviations from the strategic asset allocation; neither is random. Unintended departures from the policy weights are drift or implementation slippage, which rebalancing is meant to correct, not a recognized allocation strategy.
rationales.B: Dynamic asset allocation incorporates deviations from the strategic asset allocation motivated by longer-term valuation signals or economic views, whereas tactical asset allocation acts on shorter-term views. The two are alike in being deliberate, view-driven departures from the policy weights; the horizon of the signal is what distinguishes them.
rationales.C: This reverses the distinction. Dynamic asset allocation works off longer-term signals than tactical asset allocation does, not shorter-term ones.

questions.curriculum_ref: Passive/Active Management of Asset Class Weights

questions.stem: Passive management is most likely characterized by:

options.A: Portfolio composition that does not react to changes in capital market expectations.
options.B: Returns above the asset-class average.
options.C: Unconstrained security selection with no benchmark reference.

rationales.A: Passive management is defined by the property that portfolio composition does not react to changes in the investor's capital market expectations or to information about individual investments. The word passive is used in its ordinary sense of not reacting. Indexing is the most common example, but a buy-and-hold portfolio qualifies on the same test.
rationales.B: Realized returns are not the defining feature. A passive portfolio can outperform or underperform over any given period; what makes it passive is the absence of a response to views, not the level of its return.
rationales.C: Security selection unconstrained by a benchmark sits at the most active end of the spectrum, with high active share and high tracking risk, which is the opposite of passive management.

questions.curriculum_ref: Passive/Active Management of Allocations to Asset Classes

questions.stem: Investing an equity allocation in a broad-based value equity style index most likely represents:

options.A: A purely passive approach.
options.B: A purely active approach.
options.C: An active decision implemented passively.

rationales.A: Choosing a value tilt is an active decision. It expresses a view that value stocks will outperform the broad market, and a purely passive investor holding the market-weighted opportunity set takes no such position.
rationales.B: The implementation is not active. The style index is held as published, with no security selection within it and no reaction to new information about individual holdings.
rationales.C: Indexing to a value equity style index reflects an active decision in tilting the allocation toward value, but it is passive in implementation because it involves indexing. The example shows that passive and active are not one binary: the tilt decision and the way the tilt is implemented sit on separate dimensions, and a portfolio can be active on one and passive on the other.

questions.curriculum_ref: Passive/Active Management of Allocations to Asset Classes

questions.stem: Two widely used quantitative measures of the degree of active management are most likely:

options.A: R-squared and alpha.
options.B: Tracking risk and active share.
options.C: The Sharpe ratio and the information ratio.

rationales.A: These are related metrics but not the two standard measures of the degree of active management. R-squared describes how much of a portfolio's return variation the benchmark explains, and alpha measures value added, which is an outcome of active management rather than a measure of how active the portfolio is.
rationales.B: Tracking risk, also called tracking error, and active share are the two widely known quantitative measures of the degree of active management. Each tends to increase as a portfolio moves from most passive to most active, though not in lockstep: many small off-benchmark positions can produce high active share with low tracking risk, while a few large sector bets can produce the reverse.
rationales.C: Both measure risk-adjusted performance, which is the result of active management rather than its degree. A portfolio's information ratio says nothing about how far its holdings depart from the benchmark.

questions.curriculum_ref: Passive/Active Management of Allocations to Asset Classes (Exhibit 13)

questions.stem: For a taxable investor's assets held outside tax-advantaged accounts, taxable status is most likely a factor:

options.A: Neutral between passive and active management.
options.B: In favor of active management.
options.C: In favor of passive management.

rationales.A: Taxes do not fall equally on the two approaches. Active management generates turnover, and turnover realizes gains, so the tax drag differs meaningfully between an active mandate and an indexed portfolio holding the same asset class.
rationales.B: Tax-loss harvesting is a genuine benefit of active implementation, but it is also available within indexed and tax-managed passive portfolios, and on net active management still generates more turnover, and so more realized gains, than passive management does.
rationales.C: Taxable status is generally a factor in favor of passive management for assets not held in tax-advantaged accounts, because active management involves turnover and turnover gives rise to taxes. The consideration does not carry over to assets inside tax-advantaged accounts, where realized gains are not currently taxed and the choice turns on other factors.

questions.stem: A risk parity, or equal-risk-contribution, asset allocation approach most likely:

options.A: Equalizes dollar allocations across asset classes.
options.B: Maximizes the Sharpe ratio subject to a volatility constraint.
options.C: Equalizes each asset class's expected contribution to portfolio volatility.

rationales.A: Equal dollar weights describe an equal-weighting scheme, not risk parity. Because asset classes differ in volatility and in correlation, equal dollar weights leave the most volatile class contributing far more than its share of portfolio volatility.
rationales.B: Maximizing the Sharpe ratio subject to a volatility constraint is mean-variance optimization, which takes expected returns as inputs. Risk parity deliberately does without them, which is why it appeals to investors who distrust return forecasts.
rationales.C: Risk parity is a form of risk budgeting, in which the investor specifies how risk is distributed across assets without consideration of expected returns. The parity version aims for equal expected risk contributions to overall portfolio volatility from every included asset class, which in practice means holding less of the volatile, highly correlated classes and more of the stable ones, often with leverage applied to lift the expected return of the resulting low-volatility mix.

drills.los_text: discuss strategic considerations in rebalancing asset allocations

questions.stem: Rebalancing, as the term is used in industry practice, is best described as:

options.A: Portfolio adjustments triggered by price changes that move the asset mix off target.
options.B: Any portfolio adjustment, including tactical shifts and responses to new expectations.
options.C: Manager replacements made in response to underperformance.

rationales.A: Industry practice reserves the term rebalancing for portfolio adjustments triggered by price changes, which cause the actual asset mix to deviate from the target weights. Other portfolio adjustments, even systematic ones, are not rebalancing, so the trigger rather than the trade is what identifies it.
rationales.B: Tactical deviations and changes driven by revised capital market expectations are discretionary responses to views, not rebalancing. Grouping them under the same label would blur the difference between restoring the policy mix and deliberately departing from it.
rationales.C: Replacing a manager is a change in how an asset class is implemented and leaves the asset mix at its existing weights, so it falls outside rebalancing.

questions.stem: Rebalancing a portfolio to its target weights is most likely:

options.A: A momentum-following approach.
options.B: A passive maintenance activity with no market view.
options.C: A contrarian approach.

rationales.A: Rebalancing sells the asset classes that have risen and buys those that have fallen, which is the opposite of following momentum. A momentum strategy would add to the winners and cut the losers.
rationales.B: Rebalancing is not free of a view. Restoring the target weights after a relative price move implicitly expresses a mean-reversion view, since it is a bet that the recent relative performance will not persist.
rationales.C: Because rebalancing buys what has fallen and sells what has risen, it is countercyclical and therefore fundamentally a contrarian investment approach. Behavioral finance explains why it is uncomfortable to carry out: it requires adding to positions precisely when recent results and prevailing sentiment argue against them, which is why disciplined rebalancing policies are set in advance.

questions.stem: Of the following claims about the width of a portfolio's rebalancing ranges, the one that is least likely correct is:

options.A: Greater risk aversion implies tighter ranges.
options.B: Higher transaction costs imply wider ranges.
options.C: Higher expected returns imply wider ranges.

rationales.A: Risk aversion is one of the strategic considerations in setting range width, and the direction given here is right: a more risk-averse investor tolerates less deviation from the target allocation, so the band around each target weight is set tighter. Because the claim is correct, it is not the exception the question asks for.
rationales.B: Transaction costs are the cost-side consideration, and the direction given here is right: the higher the cost of trading an asset, the wider the no-trade band, because small deviations are not worth the cost of correcting them. Because the claim is correct, it is not the exception the question asks for.
rationales.C: Expected return is not one of the strategic considerations for range width. The considerations are transaction costs, risk aversion, correlation with the rest of the portfolio, beliefs about momentum versus mean reversion, asset illiquidity, the availability of derivatives, and taxes. Expected return drives the strategic target weight itself, not the width of the band around that weight, so no relationship running from higher expected return to wider ranges is established.

questions.stem: Under a cost-benefit approach to rebalancing, an asset class that is more highly correlated with the rest of the portfolio most likely merits:

options.A: a tighter range than a less-correlated asset.
options.B: no change in range relative to a less-correlated asset.
options.C: a wider range than a less-correlated asset.

rationales.A: This reverses the relationship. A tighter range is appropriate for an asset that is a poor substitute for the balance of the portfolio, where a given deviation moves portfolio risk a great deal. A highly correlated asset is the closer substitute, so tightening its range spends transaction costs to control a risk that is barely changing.
rationales.B: Correlation is one of the relevant strategic considerations, so it does affect the range chosen. Under a cost-benefit approach, the degree of substitutability between an asset and the balance of the portfolio is precisely what determines how much drift can be tolerated before a trade is worth its cost.
rationales.C: An asset more highly correlated with the rest of the portfolio merits a wider rebalancing range, because it is closer to being a substitute for the balance of the portfolio and larger deviations from its target therefore have less impact on total portfolio risk. The benefit of correcting the deviation is small relative to the transaction costs incurred, which argues for a wider no-trade band.

questions.stem: The three approaches commonly used to determine the size of a rebalancing trade are most likely:

options.A: rebalancing fully, partially, or not at all.
options.B: rebalancing to target, to range edge, or halfway between.
options.C: rebalancing quarterly, semiannually, or annually.

rationales.A: Full, partial or no rebalancing describes how much of a deviation gets corrected only in the loosest terms, and not rebalancing at all is not one of the three approaches: once a range has been breached, each of the three named approaches trades. The approaches are distinguished by the point the trade targets, not by whether a trade occurs.
rationales.B: The three approaches to trade size are: rebalance back to the target weight; rebalance to the range edge, the trigger point at which the range was breached; and rebalance halfway between the range-edge trigger point and the target weight. Trading to target restores the strategic allocation but costs the most; trading to the range edge is cheapest but leaves the position at the boundary, where a further small move triggers another trade; the halfway approach is the compromise between transaction costs and closeness to target.
rationales.C: Quarterly, semiannual and annual are calendar rebalancing frequencies. They answer how often the portfolio is reviewed, not how large the trade should be once a range has been breached, and trade size is a decision separate from rebalancing frequency.

questions.stem: For a taxable portfolio, taxes as a rebalancing consideration are most likely to:

options.A: have no meaningful effect on rebalancing policy.
options.B: encourage tighter and symmetric rebalancing ranges.
options.C: discourage rebalancing and widen ranges asymmetrically.

rationales.A: Taxes are a material rebalancing consideration for a taxable investor. Realizing a gain creates a tax liability that a tax-exempt investor never faces, so a tax-aware rebalancing policy differs from a tax-indifferent one in both frequency and symmetry.
rationales.B: Taxes push in the opposite direction on both counts. Because rebalancing a taxable portfolio realizes gains and accelerates the tax, it raises the cost of trading, which argues for less frequent rebalancing and wider rather than tighter ranges. Symmetry also fails, because the tax cost of trimming an appreciated position is not the same as the cost of adding to a depreciated one.
rationales.C: Taxes are a cost of rebalancing, so they discourage rebalancing and encourage wider rebalancing ranges, in the same way higher transaction costs do. They also make the ranges asymmetric: selling an appreciated asset realizes a taxable gain, while the loss side can be harvested for a tax benefit, so the band is not set symmetrically around the target weight.

questions.stem: An investor who believes that asset returns mean-revert is most likely to set:

options.A: rebalancing ranges unaffected by that belief.
options.B: tighter rebalancing ranges.
options.C: wider rebalancing ranges.

rationales.A: Beliefs about how returns behave over time feed directly into the choice of range width, so this belief is not neutral. Momentum and mean reversion are both listed considerations and they imply opposite choices of range width.
rationales.B: A belief in momentum favors wider rebalancing ranges, whereas a belief in mean reversion encourages tighter ranges. If prices mean-revert, a position that has drifted above its target is likely to give the gain back, so moving it back to target sooner captures the reversion rather than waiting for it to be given up.
rationales.C: Wider ranges follow from a belief in momentum, not mean reversion. If a position that has risen is likely to keep rising, letting it run before trading back to target captures the trend instead of cutting it short.
